question: What’s the difference between proroguing and dissolving Canada’s Parliament?
generated_answer: The Prime Minister can ask the Governor General to prorogue Parliament, which means suspending it without dissolving it. You can think of it as a “reset” button. When Parliament is prorogued, all legislation that hasn’t received Royal Assent dies on the Order Paper. This means that any bills that haven’t been passed by the Senate and the House of Commons will need to be reintroduced when Parliament resumes. The Prime Minister can also ask the Governor General to dissolve Parliament, which means ending the current session and triggering a federal election. The Governor General can only grant this request in a time of political crisis, such as a non-confidence vote in the government. When Parliament is dissolved, all legislation that hasn’t received Royal Assent dies on the Order Paper. This means that any bills that haven’t been passed by the Senate and the House of Commons will need to be reintroduced when Parliament resumes. The difference between proroguing and dissolving Parliament is that proroguing is a temporary suspension of Parliament, while dissolving Parliament is a permanent end to the current session. Proroguing can be used to reset the legislative process, while dissolving Parliament is a more drastic measure that can only be used in a time of political crisis.
